title: Evaluating the uptake and impact of an adapted breast cancer risk assessment pathway in primary care amongst South Asian and Black women
official: PREVENT-Breast: Evaluating the uptake and impact of an adapted breast cancer risk assessment pathway in primary care amongst South Asian and Black women
summary:
Background and study aims
Breast cancer is the most common cancer affecting women in the UK. Some women have a higher chance of developing breast cancer because of a combination of factors, including their family history, lifestyle, hormonal factors and genetic factors. However, many women under 50 do not know that they may be at increased risk.
The PREVENT-Breast study is looking at whether offering women a breast cancer risk assessment through their GP practice can help identify women who may be at increased risk of breast cancer. The study is particularly focused on South Asian and Black women, as previous research has shown that these groups are less likely to take up breast cancer risk assessment.
The aim is to find out whether taking part in breast cancer risk assessment is acceptable and useful to women.

Who can participate?
Women may be eligible to take part if they:
•	are aged 40–49 years
•	were assigned female at birth
•	are registered with a participating GP practice
•	are recorded in their GP records as being of South Asian or Black ethnic background

Women cannot take part if, for example, they have previously had breast or ovarian cancer, have previously been tested for a high-risk breast cancer genetic mutation, or have already taken part in certain related studies. The research team will check eligibility before women are enrolled.

What does the study involve?
Women who are eligible will receive an invitation from their GP practice. If they decide to take part, they will first complete an online consent form and a short questionnaire.
They will then complete an online breast cancer risk assessment called MyCanRisk. This asks about factors such as family history, lifestyle and hormonal factors. Participants will also be offered the option of providing a saliva sample. This is optional. If they agree, the sample will be used to look at common genetic factors associated with breast cancer risk. Women who do not wish to provide a saliva sample can still take part in the study and have their risk estimated using the other information they provide.
The information collected will be used to calculate an individual estimate of breast cancer risk using the CanRisk tool. Participants will receive their results, together with information about breast awareness. Women whose results indicate a moderate or high risk will be offered the opportunity to discuss their results with their GP and/or be referred to appropriate specialist services.
Participants will also be asked to complete follow-up questionnaires approximately 1 month and 3 months after receiving their risk assessment. These will ask about their understanding of their risk, their experience of the study, and whether the risk assessment has affected their views or behaviour.
Participants will be invited to take part in an optional interview about their experience of the study. Interviews can take place online or in person, depending on the participant's preference.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There may be no direct benefit from taking part in the research. However, participants may benefit from learning more about their individual risk of developing breast cancer. If their assessment shows that they are at increased risk, they may be offered further discussion or referral for appropriate risk management, such as enhanced breast screening or specialist assessment.
Taking part may also help researchers understand how breast cancer risk assessment can be made more accessible and acceptable to South Asian and Black women and may help improve services in the future.
The study involves some time and effort, including completing questionnaires and the MyCanRisk assessment and, if chosen, providing a saliva sample. Some of the questions ask about family history and cancer risk, and thinking about these issues or receiving information about personal breast cancer risk may cause some women to feel worried or uncomfortable. The study specifically measures cancer-related worry and the psychological impact of risk assessment as part of its follow-up.
If a participant takes part in an interview, they can stop the interview at any time or choose not to answer a particular question. Although distress is not expected, information and support procedures are in place should a participant become uncomfortable.
Taking part is voluntary, and participants can withdraw from the study at any time.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being run through GP practices in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and Manchester. It is expected to involve approximately 6–9 GP practices across these areas.
The study is led by researchers at the University of Cambridge and the University of Manchester. The sponsors are the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
Participant recruitment at each participating practice will continue for up to four months or until 120 women have been recruited.
Participants will then be followed for at least 3 months after receiving their risk assessment, with some information from health records collected up to 6 months after the assessment.
Therefore, an individual participant's involvement is expected to extend over several months, although the overall study will run for longer to allow recruitment and follow-up across all participating GP practices.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by Cancer Research UK International Alliance for Cancer Early Detection (ACED). Additional support is provided through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Manchester Biomedical Research Centre for some members of the research team.

Who is the main contact?
If you have questions about the study, you can contact the research team:
Cambridge: Amy Lafont, Study Co-ordinator, University of Cambridge, asg55@cam.ac.uk
Manchester: Helen Morley, Research Associate, University of Manchester, helen.morley@manchester.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Female sex as defined at birth
2. Aged 40-49 years at the time of invitation
3. Registered with a participating general practice (Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, or Manchester)
4. Identified in their medical records as South Asian or Black ethnic background
Exclusion criteria:
1. Have an entry in their medical records showing a personal history of breast or ovarian cancer
2. Have an entry in their medical records showing a previous diagnosis of metastatic cancer or entry on the palliative care register
3. Have an entry in their medical records showing they have given prior notification of dissent to research
4. Self-report that they have previously been tested for a high-risk mutation for breast cancer
5. Self-report that they have already participated in the CanRisk-GP or BCAN-RAY studies
6. Self-report that they have undergone or are undergoing hormonal treatment for gender reassignment
